title: Fourteen years to walk on water
hookLine: a man spends fourteen years learning to walk on water, and Hindu teachers say even real powers stand in the way
carry: the powers are obstacles, not the goal

cards: Ramakrishna, the nineteenth-century saint of Bengal, liked to tell a story. A man goes off alone to the forest and practices hard for fourteen years. At last he can walk on water.
Overjoyed, he hurries to his teacher to show him. And the teacher says, gently: my poor child. What took you fourteen years, ordinary people do for a penny.
They pay the boatman. Ramakrishna's point wasn't that the power was fake. It was that it was beside the point.

teach.b: Patanjali says the same thing, right in the middle of his list of powers. Sutra 3.37: te samadhav upasarga vyutthane siddhayah. These are obstacles in samadhi; to the outward-turned mind, they're powers.
Siddhi means an accomplishment. Upasarga means an obstacle, a trouble that comes at you.
Patanjali uses both words for the very same things. The difference is where you stand. Facing the world, hearing what no one else can hear looks like a prize.
In samadhi, it's one more thing to look at, when the whole point was to rest as the seer. And it isn't only Patanjali.

teach.h: KRISHNA TO UDDHAVA: A WASTE OF TIME.
teach.b: In the Bhagavata, in his last long talk with his friend Uddhava, Krishna lists eighteen powers a yogi can gain, and then says it outright: for one who is seeking me, these are obstacles, and a waste of time.
That's the teaching, in the yoga schools and the devotional ones alike.

teach.h: THE POWERS ARE OBSTACLES, NOT THE GOAL.
teach.b: The goal is moksha, freedom, or God himself. Not powers. Notice Patanjali doesn't call them fake.
He keeps listing them for the rest of book three. He just tells you plainly what they cost if you chase them. Today the powers look smaller: followers, being impressive, the clever answer.
Ramakrishna would ask the same question about those. Did it take you fourteen years to cross a river you could have crossed for a penny?

how: Teachers in Hindu yoga and devotional lineages quote sutra 3.37, and Krishna's words to Uddhava in the Bhagavata, to warn students against chasing powers; the aim is moksha, or God, not the abilities that may come along the way.

o: an obstacle, a trouble that comes at you
a blessing that comes after deep prayer
a vow to give up all worldly power

games.q: powers and the point — tap the pairs.

s: Patanjali says the powers are fake
he keeps listing them; he says they're obstacles in samadhi.
in the Bhagavata, Krishna calls the powers obstacles for one who seeks him
he lists eighteen, then tells Uddhava they're obstacles and a waste of time.
in Hindu teaching, gaining powers is the goal of yoga
the goal is moksha, freedom, or God; the powers can get in the way.

games.q: deep in practice, you start hearing sounds no one else can hear. by sutra 3.37, what are you facing?
o: an obstacle to absorption, however impressive.
a sign you should stop practicing.
games.why: 3.37: obstacles in samadhi, powers only to the outward mind. Krishna tells Uddhava the same: for one who seeks me, a waste of time.

practice: Rest on the breath, or on a name of God if you pray. Sooner or later a pleasing thought arrives: something you did well, a compliment, a clever idea. Notice how it tugs, wanting to be looked at.
Don't push it away. Nod to it, like the boatman's penny, and come back to the breath, or the name.

wordCard.voice: Upasarga, an obstacle, a trouble that comes at you. In the outward mind the powers are accomplishments; in absorption, they're in the way.

orig.note: Sanskrit upasarga: an obstacle, a trouble that comes upon you; in 3.37, what the powers are in samādhi.

carryVoice: Your line: the powers are obstacles, not the goal. Freedom is the goal. See you tomorrow.
